doc.title: Roswell Rudd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Father's 78 records: Armstrong, Teagarden, Ellington, Goodman
summary: Rudd recalls the first music he heard, his father's 78s of Chicago and swing players, which he danced to as a child.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah. My father and those records that I was telling you about were the first music that I heard, in the home. And I think basically that’s what it was, there was Louis Armstrong and Jelly Roll Morton and some New Orleans characters in there too, but I think mainly what I remember best it seems that he had the most records of people like Jack Teagarden, Max Kaminsky, Bud Freeman, the Chicago guys, Duke Ellington in the ‘30s kind of records, late ‘20s and ‘30s. Because don’t forget, I wasn’t born until ‘35 so when I started dancing and prancing around the room while my father was drumming to these records, those were the ones. I mean those were the au courant 78s. We weren’t actually going back, that’s when they were.
That’s right. That was the sound of the times.
Would his collection include the swing bands, a la Glenn Miller or was that a little too commercial?
Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman Trio, Benny Goodman Quartet, yeah, I remember those distinctly. Yeah those are good.
